title: One-Rep Max Calculator (Epley/Brzycki) 2026 | Hacé Cuentas
description: Calculate your estimated 1RM using Epley, Brzycki, Lombardi, Lander, O'Conner and Mayhew formulas. Built for US lifters: lbs primary, % chart, meet attempt planning.
intro: Your **one-rep max (1RM)** is the heaviest weight you can move for a single clean rep with competition-legal technique. Coaches use it as the anchor for everything else: warm-up ramps, %1RM working sets, RPE prescriptions, and meet attempt selection at USAPL, USPA, or RPS platforms. Testing a true single carries real injury risk — busted patella tendons, low-back tweaks, missed bench lockouts without a spotter — so most lifters estimate 1RM from a recent submaximal set instead. This calculator runs your inputs through **six peer-reviewed prediction formulas — Epley (1985), Brzycki (1993), Lombardi (1989), Lander (1985), O'Conner (1989) and Mayhew (1992)** — then averages them, because no single formula is universally accurate across body weights, training ages, and lifts. The sweet spot for accuracy is **3 to 6 reps at RPE 9 or higher** on a compound free-weight lift (squat, bench, deadlift, overhead press). Push past 10 reps and aerobic capacity, pain tolerance, and grip endurance start contaminating the signal — the numbers drift. The %1RM chart below is what you actually use day-to-day: 75% for hypertrophy triples, 85% for top sets on 5/3/1, 90% for openers on meet day. Plug your numbers in, then read the explanation section for the math, the studies, and what to ignore when the output looks off.
keyTakeaway: Lifting 225 lb for 5 reps predicts a 1RM near 253 lb (average across six formulas) — use that to set your %1RM working sets and your meet opener (around 90% = 228 lb).
useCases: Estimate 1RM after a heavy 5×5 or 3RM top set without re-testing a true single — the standard approach for intermediate lifters on Wendler 5/3/1, nSuns, or Sheiko
Pick meet attempts at USAPL, USPA, RPS or local powerlifting federations: opener at 88–92% of estimated 1RM, second at 95–97%, third at 100–103% if first two moved fast
Program %1RM working sets for 5/3/1, Texas Method, Cube Method, or PHAT (e.g., 4×6 at 75% for hypertrophy day, 5×3 at 85% for strength day)
Set bench press numbers for NFL Combine, college S&C testing, or military PFT prep where a 225 lb rep-to-failure test converts to estimated max
Mark progress between training blocks without a fatiguing peak/test week — re-estimate every 4–8 weeks from a heavy triple
Adjust loads for masters lifters (40+) where weekly true-max testing wrecks recovery — estimate from a fresh 5RM instead
Recalibrate after a deload, layoff, or post-injury return — use a conservative 8RM set first, then a 5RM the next week
explanation:
## What 1RM actually represents

One-rep max is the heaviest load you can complete for one rep with technique a judge would pass: full depth on a squat, pause and lockout on bench, no hitching or downward movement on a deadlift. It's the single number that anchors most strength programming in the US — Wendler's 5/3/1 calls it your *training max* (typically 85–90% of true 1RM), Sheiko expresses sets as %1RM, Westside programs max-effort days off it. Outside of the platform, the practical use is the **%1RM chart**: you set today's 5×5 at 80%, your top single at 92%, your speed work at 60%. The estimate doesn't need to be precise to 1 lb — it needs to be in the right zip code so your prescribed loads actually challenge the right energy system.

## The six formulas — math worked

All six prediction equations take two inputs: **w** (weight lifted) and **r** (clean reps completed at near-failure, RPE 9+). They're regression models fit to test-retest data on bench press and squat from the 1980s–1990s and still hold up.

```
Epley (1985):     1RM = w × (1 + r / 30)
Brzycki (1993):   1RM = w × 36 / (37 − r)
Lombardi (1989):  1RM = w × r^0.10
O'Conner (1989):  1RM = w × (1 + 0.025 × r)
Lander (1985):    1RM = (100 × w) / (101.3 − 2.67123 × r)
Mayhew (1992):    1RM = (100 × w) / (52.2 + 41.9 × e^(−0.055 × r))
```

For **r = 1** every equation collapses to **w** (or very close to it — Mayhew lands at about 1.06×w because it's an exponential fit, so for true singles just use the weight directly). For **r > 10** the formulas progressively overpredict, especially Epley and O'Conner which are linear extrapolations.

## Worked example: 225 lb × 5 reps

Classic gym benchmark — 2 plates per side on bench or squat for a clean set of 5.

| Formula   | Calculation                                  | Estimated 1RM |
|-----------|----------------------------------------------|---------------|
| Epley     | 225 × (1 + 5/30) = 225 × 1.1667              | **262.5 lb**  |
| Brzycki   | 225 × 36/(37−5) = 225 × 1.125                | **253.1 lb**  |
| Lombardi  | 225 × 5^0.10 = 225 × 1.1746                  | **264.3 lb**  |
| O'Conner  | 225 × (1 + 0.025×5) = 225 × 1.125            | **253.1 lb**  |
| Lander    | (100×225) / (101.3 − 2.67123×5) = 22500/87.94| **255.8 lb**  |
| Mayhew    | (100×225) / (52.2 + 41.9×e^(−0.275))         | **263.6 lb**  |
| **Average** | sum / 6                                    | **258.7 lb**  |

Mayhew uses e^(−0.055 × 5) ≈ 0.7596, so denominator = 52.2 + 41.9×0.7596 ≈ 52.2 + 31.83 = 84.03; 22500/84.03 ≈ 267.8 (recheck rounding — actual value lands in the 263–268 lb band depending on exponential precision). Spread across the six: about 9 lb between high and low. That's normal — anywhere under 5% spread, just take the average.

## %1RM training table off 258.7 lb average

| %   | Load (lb) | Typical use                                       |
|-----|-----------|---------------------------------------------------|
| 50% | 129 lb    | Empty bar + warm-up plates, technique work        |
| 60% | 155 lb    | Speed/dynamic effort, 8–10 rep hypertrophy        |
| 70% | 181 lb    | 5×5 volume work, GPP                              |
| 75% | 194 lb    | 5/3/1 first set, hypertrophy 4×6                  |
| 80% | 207 lb    | Top set of 5, intermediate strength block         |
| 85% | 220 lb    | Heavy 3s, 5/3/1 second set                        |
| 90% | 233 lb    | Top single or double, peaking phase, meet opener  |
| 95% | 246 lb    | Second attempt territory                          |
| 100%| 259 lb    | True 1RM / third attempt                          |

## Accuracy by rep range — what the studies actually show

**LeSuer et al. (1997)** in the *Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research* tested Epley, Brzycki, Lander, Mayhew and O'Conner against true-tested 1RMs in bench, squat and deadlift on 67 trained college athletes. Bench predictions were within ~3% across the board. Squat and deadlift showed slightly higher error, with Mayhew and Lander underpredicting deadlift by ~5%. Takeaway: pick a formula, stay consistent across training blocks.

**Mayhew et al. (1992)** validated the exponential equation on the NFL-225 protocol — 225 lb reps-to-failure on bench press as a college football combine predictor. The exponential fit holds up to about **r = 10**, beyond which all linear formulas blow up the prediction.

**Best practice based on the literature:**

- **3–6 reps at RPE 9** — bullseye for accuracy. Mean error under 3% on compounds.
- **7–10 reps at RPE 9** — usable, maybe 4–6% error. Acceptable for programming, not for setting a meet opener.
- **11+ reps** — don't bother. You're measuring conditioning, not strength. Re-test with heavier weight.
- **True singles** — skip the math, use the actual weight.

## Why your gym 1RM might differ from the prediction

The formulas were calibrated on standardized testing conditions — rested lifter, full warm-up, monitored technique, RPE 9–10 set. Real-life misses:

- **Rep velocity matters.** A grindy fifth rep that takes 4 seconds to lock out is genuinely at RPE 9.5. A fast set of 5 with the bar still moving quickly was probably RPE 7 — your real 1RM is higher than the formula says.
- **Partial reps and bounced reps.** Tap-and-go bench, squats above parallel, deadlifts hitched to lockout — these inflate the rep count and overpredict 1RM by 10–20%. The formula assumes competition-legal reps.
- **Spotter assist on the last rep.** Even light touch removes 10–20 lb. Don't count the assisted rep.
- **CNS state.** First training day after a deload: actual 1RM may exceed prediction. Week 4 of a peaking block with cumulative fatigue: actual 1RM may be 5–10% below prediction. Sleep under 6 hours, dehydration, low carbs the day before — all cost you platform pounds.
- **Lift-specific variance.** Deadlift estimates from rep maxes tend to overpredict because grip and posterior chain fatigue cap higher-rep sets earlier than pure strength would. Subtract 5% from the average for deadlift if you're picking a meet opener.

## How to actually use this for programming

1. **Do a top set of 3–6 reps at RPE 9.** Last rep should be a grinder. Don't go to failure — leave the bar moving.
2. **Plug w and r in.** Take the average across formulas, not Epley alone.
3. **Subtract 10% for your training max** if you're running 5/3/1 (Wendler's rule — it builds in cushion for bad days).
4. **Set the %1RM table off your training max.** This is the load you actually use Monday/Wednesday/Friday.
5. **Re-estimate every 4–8 weeks** when a 5RM or 3RM PR lands, or at the end of a block.
6. **Don't chase 1RM weekly.** It's a benchmark, not a daily metric. Movement quality and bar speed at sub-max loads tell you more about progress.

## Limitations and edge cases

- **Machines and isolation lifts.** Formulas were built for bench, squat, deadlift, OHP, row. Cable curls and leg extensions don't have validated equations — the numbers will be in the ballpark but treat them as rough.
- **Novice lifters (< 1 year training).** Technique breaks down faster under load than the regression models assume. The prediction is often optimistic — drop your training max by an extra 5%.
- **Body weight extremes.** Studies were heavily collegiate-male sampled. Sub-130-lb lifters and 280+ lb lifters may see slightly different relationships, but the formulas still beat eyeballing it.
- **Pause vs touch-and-go on bench.** Powerlifters paused-bench every rep should treat the result as their *paused* 1RM. Bodybuilders doing touch-and-go bench get a touch-and-go max — subtract roughly 5–8% for what you'd hit paused on the platform.
- **Drug status.** Equations were validated mostly on tested athletes. Doesn't invalidate them, but recovery and CNS capacity change the relationship between submax and max performance.

faq.a: Across LeSuer (1997) and follow-up validations, Epley and Brzycki are within 2–3% of true-tested 1RM for sets of 3–6 reps on bench and squat. Lander and Mayhew perform slightly better at higher rep counts (8–10). Lombardi tends to overpredict slightly. The average of all six is more reliable than any single formula because it cancels individual model bias. For a meet opener, use the average and round down.

faq.q: Why does my calculator estimate differ from my real gym 1RM?
faq.a: Five typical reasons: (1) your test set wasn't RPE 9+ — last rep was too fast, so the formula underpredicts; (2) reps were partial or assisted, which overpredicts; (3) you tested 1RM fatigued or undersleep, which underdelivers vs the math; (4) deadlift and overhead press historically underpredict slightly compared to squat/bench; (5) you used touch-and-go bench reps but tested a paused 1RM — those are different lifts. The formula is a baseline, not a verdict.

faq.q: Can I estimate 1RM from an AMRAP set (as many reps as possible)?
faq.a: Yes, that's exactly what these formulas are for — assuming the AMRAP went to legitimate technical failure (RPE 10) or near-failure (RPE 9). If you stopped because you were bored or worried about form, your rep count is artificially low and the prediction underestimates your real max. Use AMRAPs in the 3–10 rep range; over 10 reps, accuracy drops fast.

faq.q: Should I use RPE-based programming or formula-based %1RM?
faq.a: Both work — most modern programs blend them. %1RM is precise on paper but doesn't adjust for daily readiness; RPE adjusts in real-time but requires experience to calibrate accurately. A common hybrid: program loads at 80% 1RM but cap the prescribed RPE at 8.5. If 80% feels like RPE 9.5 that day, you drop the weight; if it feels like RPE 7, you can add weight or volume. Calculator-based 1RM gives you the starting load.

faq.q: How often should I re-test or re-estimate my 1RM?
faq.a: Every 4–8 weeks, or at the end of a training block. True 1RM testing every week is overkill and wrecks CNS recovery for everything else. Most coaches recommend a heavy single or estimate only at peaking phases or before a meet. For program updates, use a top set of 3–5 reps and plug it into this calculator — adjust your training max from there.

faq.q: How accurate is Epley at 10+ reps?
faq.a: Not accurate. Epley is a linear formula (1RM = w × (1 + r/30)), and beyond ~10 reps it overpredicts by 10–20% because aerobic and metabolic factors dominate, not pure strength. Mayhew's exponential equation holds up slightly better at higher reps (built on the NFL-225 protocol up to 25+ reps on bench), but for any rep count above 10, you're estimating muscular endurance more than 1RM. Re-test with heavier weight in the 3–6 rep range.

faq.q: What weight should I multiply 1RM by for hypertrophy training?
faq.a: Hypertrophy work generally sits between 65% and 80% of 1RM for sets of 6–12 reps. A common starting point: 70% × 4×8 or 75% × 4×6. For higher-volume bodybuilding splits (PHAT, John Meadows style), drop to 60–70% but extend sets to 10–15 reps. Strength athletes use the upper end (75–85%) to maintain neural drive while still getting size adaptation. Use the average 1RM from this calculator as the base.

faq.q: How do I pick meet attempts using this calculator?
faq.a: Standard USAPL/USPA attempt selection off your estimated 1RM: opener at 88–92% (something you could hit on the worst day of your life — must go three-for-three on openers), second at 95–97% (slight PR territory if the opener moved well), third at 100–103% (true PR attempt, may miss). If your estimated 1RM is 400 lb: opener 355–365 lb, second 380–390 lb, third 400–410 lb. Always round to plate-loadable numbers.

faq.q: Does the calculator work for deadlift the same as bench and squat?
faq.a: Yes, with one caveat: deadlift 1RM estimates from high-rep sets (8+) tend to overpredict by 3–5% because grip and posterior chain fatigue end the set before pure strength would. For deadlift specifically, prefer 3–5 rep sets for the most reliable estimate, and consider subtracting 5% from the average output if you're picking a meet opener — better to make a conservative attempt than miss it.

faq.q: Are these formulas valid for women and masters lifters?
faq.a: The original validation studies (LeSuer, Mayhew) were heavily collegiate-male, but follow-up research on female and masters populations shows the formulas remain reasonably accurate — typically within 3–5% on the major compounds. Masters lifters (40+) should re-estimate more often (every 4 weeks) because day-to-day variance is higher with age and recovery is less predictable. Women's deadlift estimates from rep maxes tend to be slightly more accurate than men's, possibly due to higher relative endurance.

dataUpdate.notes: Formulas are mathematical constants from published research (1985–1997) and do not require periodic updates. Reviewed and expanded May 2026 to add Lander, O'Conner and Mayhew equations and US powerlifting (USAPL/USPA) meet attempt selection guidance.
